evidences.title: Usain Bolt returns to London with a shadow hanging over the 100m | Usain Bolt | The Guardian
evidences.content:
Usually when Usain Bolt is asked about drugs, his answers become mantras. He is more tested than other athletes. He is clean. His times can be trusted. But in the wake of last week's positive tests for Tyson Gay and Asafa Powell, Bolt appeared to understand that off-the-peg responses were not enough; a situation this worrying for the sport demanded bespoke tailoring.

And Bolt attempted to provide it by insisting that his world records were the logical consequences of genetics and a decade of hard graft. "I was made to inspire people and made to run," he insisted. "I was given a gift and that's what I do. I know I'm clean."

Bolt also drew upon his performances as a callow, gangly teenager, which included running 19.93sec in the 200m as a 17-year-old, to add greater weight to his words. "How long have you been following Usain Bolt?" he asked one interrogator. "If you've been following me since 2002 you would know I've been doing phenomenal things since I was 15. I was the youngest person to win the world juniors. I ran the world youth record at 17.

"I've broken every record there is in every event I've ever done. I've proven myself since I was 15. I was always going to be great."

In case the world needed reminding, Bolt reiterated that his blood is frequently extracted and examined by anti-doping agents. "I got tested the day before yesterday. It's just a part of the routine," he said matter-of-factly, as if he was talking about drawing the curtains in the morning.

But Bolt admitted that Jamaican athletics' five recent positive drugs tests had not helped the sport, or the image of his country.

"As Jamaicans we're very proud of our athletes so it's kind of rough," he said. Hopefully this will work out. I just have to continue working hard and bring glory to my country."

Bolt talked a lot about hard work and his numbing training regime  "all I do is work really, all I do is train and sleep and do video games. That's my routine every day"  but he admitted he was looking forward to racing again at London's Olympic Stadium.

Last year he won three Olympic gold medals, in the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay as well as running 9.63sec, the second fastest 100m time in history. But Bolt has been more conventional flier than supersonic jet plane this year. Two of the athletes he faces  the Jamaican Nesta Carter and Britain's James Dasaolu  have run faster than him in 2013.

Not that Bolt is concerned. "I never try to worry about times," he said. "I'm in great shape. I could have run faster at my national championships. I've been working hard. I've gone through two and a half weeks of just solid training  everything there is I needed to work on. I've been working on my core work, back exercises. I'm looking forward to this 100m: I'm ready and I'm ready to go."

And while there is no Gay or Powell or Justin Gatlin, Bolt still faces a stacked field. Every athlete in the race has run under 10 seconds, with Carter, the fifth fastest man in history, running 9.87sec this season.

Kim Collins and Dwain Chambers may be the wrong side of 35 but they have straddled the 10-second barrier in 2013. And while the American Mike Rodgers is not someone those in the bleachers will instinctively recognise, he has a 9.85sec personal best. Meanwhile his compatriot Rakieem Salaam, who at 23 has time on his side, has run 9.97sec.

But it is Dasaolu, Britain's late bloomer who smashed the 10-second barrier in Birmingham a fortnight ago, who provides Bolt's most intriguing opponent.

The Jamaican was so relaxed in meeting the world's media that he wore his Ray Bans so they covered the back of his head rather than his eyes, and spoke in seductive, sonorous tones.

Dasaolu, meanwhile, gave off the fidgety ticks of someone about to have their passport photo taken. He was unsure about whether to smile or stay stoic; to show teeth or pursed lips. You fear for his hamstrings if he is this tight on Friday.

"I know it's going to be a tough race against the quickest man in history, a six-time Olympic champion," said Dasaolu. "But this is what I work hard for every day that I wake up."

The 25-year-old Dasaolu certainly deserves his chance. He has made huge strides since moving to Loughborough to train with Steve Fudge in January 2012. The strains and pains and niggles that kept rudely interrupting his career have subsided, and his personal best of 9.91sec is not to be sniffed at. Except, perhaps, if you're the fastest man on the planet. "I really enjoy competing in London," said Bolt, with joyous relish.

"It's like competing in Jamaica because a lot of Jamaicans come to support me." He mentioned last year's Olympics with slightly less affection, but noted that "it was a chance to stamp my class". Expect him to do the same again on Friday.

Anniversary Games men's 100m, 9.48pm. Live on BBC2
